content: The International Association for the Surgery of Trauma and Surgical Intensive Care (IATSIC) was established in 1988 with the aim of creating a platform for the exchange of information and the development of new knowledge in trauma surgery and surgical intensive care. This is achieved through clinical experience, laboratory research, scientific meetings, publications, and training courses. IATSIC operates as an integrated society within the International Society of Surgery (ISS/SIC), which was founded in 1902 and has over 3,000 members across 80 countries. IATSIC itself has 270 members from 53 countries, representing every continent. Its members are surgeons with a significant interest and active practice in trauma surgery and/or surgical intensive care, and contributions to scientific literature in these fields are a key factor in determining membership. The World Health Organization (WHO), established in 1948 as a specialized agency of the United Nations, serves as the directing and coordinating authority for international health matters and public health. One of WHO's constitutional functions is to provide objective and reliable information and advice on human health. This is achieved through an extensive program of publications, which aim to support national health strategies and address pressing public health concerns globally. WHO publications include practical manuals, handbooks, training materials, internationally applicable guidelines, reviews of health policies and research, and consensus reports offering technical advice and recommendations for decision-makers. These publications are closely aligned with WHO's priority activities, such as disease prevention and control, equitable health system development, and health promotion for individuals and communities. The Guidelines for Essential Trauma Care were developed collaboratively by WHO and IATSIC, along with input from other international and national societies and experts in trauma care worldwide. These guidelines aim to reduce disparities in trauma care outcomes by establishing achievable and affordable standards for injury care globally. They outline essential trauma services that are considered feasible in virtually all settings and detail the human and physical resources required to provide these services. The guidelines emphasize the importance of improved organization and planning of trauma care services to achieve better outcomes for injured patients, even in resource-limited settings. They also highlight the cost-effectiveness, feasibility, and sustainability of these improvements. Trauma is a significant global health problem, causing 16,000 deaths daily and accounting for 16% of the global disease burden. The burden of injury-related death and disability is particularly high in lowand middle-income countries, where 90% of the total injury burden occurs. Addressing this challenge requires efforts to improve both injury prevention and trauma care. The guidelines provide a resource matrix detailing the human and physical resources needed for optimal trauma care at various levels of health facilities, from rural health posts to tertiary care centers. They also include recommendations for training, performance improvement, trauma team organization, and hospital inspection to strengthen trauma care systems globally. The guidelines were developed with input from clinicians actively involved in trauma care in diverse settings, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. They aim to address disparities in trauma outcomes by improving the organization of trauma care services, which has been shown to be a cost-effective way to enhance patient outcomes. The guidelines are intended for use by healthcare planners, administrators, and clinicians to advocate for and implement improvements in trauma care resources and services. By providing a template for organizing and strengthening trauma treatment systems, the guidelines aim to facilitate better outcomes for injured patients worldwide.
